summary: This informational document describes a framework for preventing the transient loops that can occur in link-state routing when topology changes. It does so by correctly ordering the forwarding information base (FIB) updates on routers. It suits planned shutdowns, restarts, and metric changes, and can work alongside fast reroute.

eli5.summary: When roads change, drivers need to update maps in the right order or they go in circles. This sets the order so traffic does not loop.

questions: how to avoid micro-loops in link-state routing
how does ofib prevent routing loops
subtitle: Preventing packet loops by updating router forwarding tables in the right order.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails or changes in a network, routers briefly have inconsistent forwarding tables. Packets can loop between routers during this period, causing loss and disruption even when the network remains connected.
tldr.mechanism: The oFIB approach computes a rank for each router based on the topology change, then stages their forwarding table updates in order. Routers closer to the failure update first, then others in sequence, so packets always follow a consistent path.
tldr.outcome: Loop-free convergence is guaranteed for single topology changes if all routers follow the ordering. The mechanism works for managed changes (maintenance, metric updates) and can accelerate fast reroute.

facts.label: Target convergence time
facts.value: Seconds to minutes (T0 + H + rank × MAX_FIB)

facts.label: Failure scope
facts.value: Single link, router, or line card

today: RFC 6976 is Informational and remains current. It describes a framework that has been subject to simulation and one experimental deployment. Routers still use traditional convergence by default; implementations of oFIB or similar loop-free convergence mechanisms are found in some carrier deployments.

sections.title: The Transient Loop Problem
sections.content:
Link-state routing protocols like OSPF and IS-IS let each router learn the whole network topology and compute the best paths. When a link fails or changes—whether by accident or as planned maintenance—some routers learn the change before others. Until all routers have updated their forwarding information bases (FIBs), they have different ideas of the best path to a destination. Packets can bounce between routers that disagree, looping until a router updates its table or a TTL expires.

The oFIB (Ordered Forwarding Information Base) framework prevents this by controlling the order in which routers update their FIBs. Instead of letting each router update as soon as it learns the change, oFIB computes a safe schedule so that at every moment during the update, the routers have consistent enough routing that no loops occur.
sections.eli5: Each driver gets a number telling them when to update their map. If they follow the numbers, traffic never gets stuck.

sections.title: Link Down and Link Up Rules
sections.content:
The oFIB approach distinguishes between link-down events (failure or shutdown) and link-up events (restoration or new link).

When a link goes down, routers that send traffic through the affected router must update their tables before that router does. This ensures packets following an old route reach the far end of the failed link, where there is no longer a way back, so they take the new best path forward. Once upstream routers have rerouted, the affected router can safely update.

When a link comes up, the rule reverses. Routers must update before routers that will use them as the next hop to reach the new link. This way, traffic can reach the new link without first arriving at a router that has not yet learned the faster path.
sections.eli5: When a road closes, tell neighbors to find new routes first, then tell the closed road's endpoint. When a road opens, tell the endpoint first so traffic can find the shortcut.

sections.title: Computing Router Rank and Timing
sections.content:
Each router computes a rank that determines when it can safely update. For a failure, rank is the distance (in hops) from the router to the failed element in the old topology: routers closest to the failure get a lower rank and update sooner.

The actual update time is calculated as T0 + H + (rank × MAX_FIB), where T0 is when the change was announced, H is a hold-down time to let all routers hear the news, and MAX_FIB is a network-wide constant representing the maximum time to update a table. This simple formula ensures that routers waiting for a neighbor to update will not have to wait too long, so convergence happens in predictable time.
sections.eli5: Each router gets a number based on how far it is from the broken link. It waits (number × fixed time) before updating, so closer routers go first.

sections.title: State Machine and Safety Fallback
sections.content:
An oFIB-capable router moves through states: from stable, to holding (collecting change notifications), to ongoing (during the timed update window), and back to stable. During the holding and ongoing states, the router watches for events that would break the ordered process: a second failure before the first has converged, or a change affecting a different part of the topology. If such an event occurs, the router abandons oFIB and reverts to normal convergence (often called fast convergence), which happens as fast as possible but risks transient loops.

This safety fallback (called "Abandoning All Hope" in the RFC) ensures that oFIB cannot make things worse when its assumptions break.
sections.eli5: If another road closes before the first one has settled, stop the careful plan and just let everyone fix their maps right away.

sections.title: Use Cases and Limitations
sections.content:
oFIB is suited for managed, non-urgent changes: planned link shutdowns, metric changes, and scheduled maintenance. It can also accelerate fast reroute, where a protection mechanism (like MPLS FRR) instantly reroutes traffic around a failure and oFIB then manages the orderly FIB convergence afterward.

oFIB handles single failures only. If multiple independent failures happen, or if the topology diverges from the assumptions built into the rank computation, convergence reverts to normal mode. All routers in the domain must support oFIB; if some do not, the network uses normal convergence instead.
sections.eli5: Works best for planned changes and when one thing breaks at a time. If two things break or a router does not support the system, just do it the fast way.
